**On the Strangeness of Ordinary Things**

There is a Russian word, *ostranenie*, coined by the literary critic Viktor Shklovsky in 1917, that translates roughly as "making strange." Shklovsky believed that the purpose of art was to break the crust of habit that forms over our perception. We stop seeing the things we see every day. We don't look at our hands anymore; we don't taste our coffee past the third sip; we walk home along a street we could not describe if asked. Habit, Shklovsky said, "devours works, clothes, furniture, one's wife, and the fear of war." Art exists to make the stone *stony* again.

I find myself thinking about this often, because if there is one thing worth doing with attention, it is recovering the strangeness of what we've stopped noticing. Consider a few examples.

Consider the fact that you are, right now, decoding small black marks on a surface, and that these marks are causing a voice to occur inside your head — a voice that is not quite yours and not quite mine, a third thing, a collaboration. Writing is a technology so old we've forgotten it's a technology at all. But for most of human history, the idea that thought could be frozen into objects and thawed out centuries later by strangers would have seemed like sorcery. Socrates was suspicious of it. He worried, in the *Phaedrus*, that writing would atrophy memory and produce people who seemed wise without being wise. He may have been right. We only know he said this, of course, because Plato wrote it down.

Consider water. Two hydrogen atoms, one oxygen, and a set of properties so anomalous that if a chemist encountered the formula without prior knowledge, they would predict almost none of them. Water expands when it freezes — nearly everything else contracts — which means ice floats, which means lakes freeze from the top down instead of the bottom up, which means fish survive winter, which means, arguably, that complex life persisted long enough to produce someone capable of finding this surprising. It has an absurdly high heat capacity, which is why coastal cities have mild weather and why your body, mostly water, doesn't swing wildly in temperature every time you walk outside. We treat water as the definition of the ordinary — "watered down," "weak as water" — when it is closer to a cosmic stroke of luck.

Consider sleep. Every night, you voluntarily lose consciousness for hours, becoming paralyzed and hallucinating vividly, and this is considered not only normal but mandatory. Animals do it even though it makes them spectacularly vulnerable to predators, which suggests it must accomplish something so important that evolution accepted the cost of eight hours of helplessness per day. We still don't entirely know what that something is. We have theories — memory consolidation, metabolic cleanup, synaptic pruning — but the honest answer is that one-third of human life remains substantially mysterious to the species living it.

Why does this matter? Why is making the stone stony again worth anyone's time?

One answer is hedonic: a re-enchanted world is simply more pleasurable to live in. The person who can be astonished by water gets to be astonished much more often than the person who requires the Grand Canyon. Wonder becomes cheap, abundant, locally sourced.

But I think there's a deeper answer, which is that habituation is not just a perceptual phenomenon — it's a moral one. We habituate to injustices, to cruelties, to absurdities, the same way we habituate to wallpaper. The first time you encounter some entrenched unfairness, it shocks you; the hundredth time, it's just how things are. Shklovsky's contemporary, the writer who took defamiliarization furthest, was probably Tolstoy, and he used it for exactly this purpose. In one famous passage, he describes an opera from the perspective of someone who has never absorbed the conventions — people in strange clothes howling at each other while others watch — and suddenly the opera seems ridiculous. He did the same with flogging, with property, with war, describing them as a visitor from elsewhere might, stripped of the justifying haze of normalcy. Making things strange is a precondition for asking whether they should exist at all.

There's a practice hiding in this, available to anyone. Pick something you've stopped seeing and describe it as though reporting back to a civilization that has never encountered it. A handshake: two strangers approach, grip each other's appendages, and oscillate them briefly to signal the absence of weapons and the presence of goodwill. Money: humans exchange genuinely useful things — bread, labor, shelter — for tokens whose entire value consists of the shared belief that everyone else will also accept them. The belief is the asset. Birthdays: once a year, we set small fires atop a sweetened cake and the celebrated person extinguishes them with their breath, after which everyone applauds the extinguishing.

None of this is mockery. Defamiliarization done well isn't sneering at human customs; it's looking at them with the kind of attention we usually reserve for things we love. The handshake, seen freshly, is rather beautiful — a small ritual of mutual disarmament we perform dozens of times without thinking. The strangeness and the tenderness arrive together.

Shklovsky wrote his famous essay during a catastrophic period — war, revolution, scarcity — and there's something poignant about insisting, in such a moment, that the central problem of human life is that we stop noticing it. But maybe that's exactly when the insistence matters most. Habit is a kind of anesthesia, and anesthesia is useful right up until it isn't, until it numbs you to the very experiences that were the point of being alive.

So: the stone is stony. Water is bizarre. Sleep is a nightly miracle of accepted vulnerability. You are decoding marks, and a voice that belongs to neither of us is finishing this sentence in your head. None of it had to be this way, and almost none of it is ordinary, except in the narrow sense that it happens all the time — which, when you think about it, only deepens the strangeness.
